newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAFRICA MAIZE FUTURES UP ON US RALLY, TIGHT SUPPLY.
newsitem.headline: SAFRICA MAIZE FUTURES UP ON US RALLY, TIGHT SUPPLY.

text.p: South African yellow and white maize futures rose this week, boosted by tight supply in the local market and an overnight rally in Chicago, traders said on Wednesday.
The September yellow maize contract was trading five rand up at 550 rand on Wednesday while December yellow was eight higher at 595.
The white September contract was up five at 640 rand and the later-dated March contract also up five at 710.

Traders said prices were higher after Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) corn futures rallied on Tuesday when the U.S. Department of Agriculture estimated U.S. 1997 corn production of around 9.276 billion bushels -- far below the July forecast of 9.7 billion.
"It is definitely because Chicago jumped its limit," one trader said.
But the trader said a perceived tightness of supply in the domestic market -- due to increased exports -- could also be behind the increase in futures contract prices.
"Supply is becoming extremely on the tight side...It is basically because of the exports going out of the country," the trader said.
The South African Futures Exchange (Safex) said on Wednesday local prices could be higher on a weaker rand and higher exports.
"It could be because the rand is quite weak, therefore international prices are up. That would tend to put pressure on the local price.

"It could be too that there is a feeling that maybe more was exported from South Africa than was originally thought, therefore there is a bit of a squeeze on the market," Safex general manager Rod Blondin told Reuters.
On Wednesday, the rand was trading at around 4.66 to the dollar -- off last week's 4.70, the currency's lowest level against the dollar in seven months.

Market sources said last week that continued weakness in the rand may lead to more exports of South African yellow maize as prices became more attractive, shrinking the surplus anticipated for this season.

Concerns about the early and intense build-up of El Nino, which has in the past wreaked havoc with weather conditions and ravaged agricultural output, would add further support to yellow and white prices, especially in later months.

The National Maize Producers Organisation said white maize might start to be channelled to Zambia as that country's import needs rose following worse-than-expected crop damage from grey leaf spot disease.
South Africa has already exported sizeable quantities to Kenya following a drought there, keeping white prices firm amid concerns of a local shortage.
